A cutting-edge approach has been developed to identify tau decaying into non-prompt particles. It involves training a deep neural network on 10 distinct neural networks, which accurately distinguishes between tau decays and jets. This novel approach outperforms standard techniques by significantly increasing the identification efficiency. Results from testing on 2017 ALICE data show a substantial improvement in identification efficiency by a factor of 4 compared to previous methods, while maintaining similar levels of background suppression.

Future sky surveys by Rubin and Rubin-1 will generate massive datasets exceeding 1 petabyte, presenting significant challenges and opportunities for cosmology. Pinpointing supernovae types and precise redshifts from vast amounts of data will be pivotal for understanding dark energy. Our research focuses on developing efficient machine learning methods that can handle the immense volume of data. We compare three classification techniques - 1) a Bayesian Neural Network, 2) employing neural networks to train a traditional machine learning classifier, and 3) utilizing neural networks to enhance the accuracy of point-spread function modeling. We found that Bayesian Neural Networks outperform other methods in both robustness and interpretability.

Our study delves into the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering across modal interactions within solid-core photonic crystal fibers, showcasing a substantial increase, up to seven orders, in the interaction coefficient compared to single-mode silicon waveguides of similar dimensions. This discovery is facilitated by intermodal coupling, which overcomes the inherent limitations of high optical propagation loss within such fibers. Moreover, by carefully tailoring the geometry of the fiber's hole layout, substantial enhancements in the interaction coefficient can be achieved, even for fibers that support multiple modal propagation. The underlying physical principles governing intermodal coupling and modal energy dissipation are also examined in this study. The results presented can be leveraged to develop efficient, all-silicon, microstructured fibers for applications requiring high-sensitivity sensing capabilities.

The B-type Coxeter group's generators, denoted by $S$, give rise to a family of linear representations labeled by pairs $(p,q)$ of non-negative integers. This study introduces a generalization of Stembridge's basis theorem applicable to these representations. Additionally, explicit generalizations of three key Stembridge basis-associated elements are presented for a specific permutation representation known as $(p,0)$.

Two related variations of the well-known knapsack problem are the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem. Both involve selecting items to maximize a objective function while adhering to a budget constraint and a set of unique restrictions. The classical knapsack problem has been extensively studied and solved using various methods, including local search, dynamic programming, and branch-and-bound. However, due to its increased complexity, Set-Union Knapsack Problem and its associated problems are significantly harder, with the former being proven to be strongly NP-hard. Research has attempted to adapt existing algorithms for knapsack, yielding suboptimal results, prompting the need for novel solutions. This study proposes a range of efficient and effective local search algorithms for both problems. The proposed algorithms, which utilize swap- and insert-based search along with density estimation, are then evaluated through extensive numerical experiments. The outcomes demonstrate the superiority of these algorithms, particularly those combining insert-based search and density estimation, over existing benchmarks and swap- and swap-based local search methods for the Set-Union Knapsack Problem.

Churn prediction is a critical challenge in online businesses, including online gaming companies. In this project, we focused on identifying at-risk gamblers in real-time, enabling operators to implement tailored retention strategies. The dataset provided baseline customer behavior information, allowing us to develop a non-supervised model for predicting customer turnover. The model's accuracy was validated using a testing dataset, revealing that gender and deposit amount were crucial factors in turnover. The proposed solution leverages real-time data processing through a Flink-based data lake.

We are studying the Ising Field Theory in 2 dimensions with a magnetic field, and we are analyzing the theory's behavior near its critical point. When the magnetic field is extremely weak, the theory is known to have one parameterless vertex operator and depends solely on magnetic field strength at a certain energy level. In our work, we are introducing a second, magnetic-dependent vertex operator to the theory and we are calculating how this operator influences key quantities in the theory, specifically the mass and coupling constant of an excited state in the theory. We are also introducing a source for this new vertex operator to the theory, and we are analyzing how the resulting singularity in the theory's behavior as a function of magnetic field strength differs from its behavior in the absence of this source. Furthermore, we are proposing a way to regularize the source in such a way that the resulting influence on the theory is measurable and dependent solely on a non-universal constant. We are implementing numerical simulations to support our work, and we are calculating fundamental properties of the theory, and we are achieving good agreement with existing numerical and experimental data.

Our research shows that lattice-calculated transverse-momentum-dependent parton distribution functions can be converted into the light-cone standard with any target momentum fraction $x$ through large-momentum effective theory. This achievement stems from deriving a momentum expansion factorization formula that can be applied both on lattes and in proton $x$ space. This formula is backed up by effective field theory and allows for the derivation of power-suppressed corrections, and includes a set of matrix elements that can be computed on lattices. Using this method, we developed a power-suppressed correction estimate in the nucleon spin-dependent $d$-quark distribution $d^{q, \Delta}$. Furthermore, this framework provides a pathway for deriving target-momentum fraction-dependent factorization formulas and the corresponding parton distribution functions for various currents.

In the context of heavy-nuclei collisions, electrons and positrons experience electromagnetic interactions when they approach these nuclei at low transverse momentum. Specifically, when these particles interact with heavy nuclei in the framework of ultra-relativistic, heavy-ion collisions, effects such as the Coulomb potential and the electron's spin are considered significant in the approximation of the eikonal approach. Moreover, the influence of both the Coulomb potential and the electron's spin on the scattering process is analyzed in the approximation of the eikonal approach. Furthermore, the Coulomb scattering of a positron in the approximation of the eikonal approach is studied, and the influence of the electron's spin on the scattering process is also addressed. Lastly, the influence of the Coulomb potential and the electron's spin on the scattering process in the electromagnetic interaction process is evaluated based on the number of participants in the collisions at the Large Hadron Collider in a lead-lead system.

To minimize casualties, traffic management systems require advanced technologies. Current systems primarily focus on reducing cyclist accidents through traffic lights and barriers, but they are still insufficient. Current technologies mainly focus on vehicle speed, but they fail to account for important factors like driver age, experience, and other road users. In response, a video-based risk descriptor has been developed, using computer vision to analyze context and track road users, assessing various risk factors including speed, distance, and other environmental cues. The risk descriptor's effectiveness was validated through extensive video analysis, achieving high accuracy and low processing times.

A novel risk-averse method is introduced to generate robot movement plans that effectively address uncertainty. This risk-prohibiting algorithm employs the Zeno control barrier function to map out a barrier within the state space, which limits the state space to one that can be safely controlled by a robust feedback controller capable of handling uncertainty. This risk-prohibiting algorithm is based on a model of uncertainty and noise, and it uses a grid-based path planning method to restrict the robot's trajectory. Finally, the safety of the generated plans is ensured by applying the calculated path to the robot using a feedback controller. Simulation results using a mobile robot in a mobile office setting demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

A subring S of a ring R can serve as a cover for the group of units R* if it encompasses them in a finite product of ideals, the number of which is minimized at c_s(R). This minimised value is referred to as the one-dimensional covering number of R, initially introduced by Ellsworth in 1966. Generalising this in 2001, Anderson and Salami developed the concept of the n-dimensional covering number, denoted c_n(R), to apply to n-dimensional modules over the ring R, with c_1(R) equivalent to c_s(R). This work investigates the 1-dimensional covering number of commutative Artinian rings, specifically in terms of its length and a set of nilpotent and residue field covering numbers, and explores the relationship between c_1(R) and the dimension of R. Additionally, it provides upper and lower bounds for c_n(R) relative to covering numbers in a quotient ring R/Q, with Q being a prime ideal, and examines the dependence of c_n(R) on n, which is shown to be a non-increasing function, with the ultimate limit being a product of the covering numbers of the ring's simple quotient fields.

Recent studies have highlighted how deep neural networks become vulnerable to subtle, artificially manipulated inputs, known as adversarial examples. Recent efforts to defend against such attacks have focused on adversarial training, aiming to increase resilience against them. Our study presents a new perspective on the issue by investigating how the characteristics of well-trained models provide natural protection against these subtle alterations. By examining how these models generalize to similar, but slightly modified versions of their training data, we reveal that this self-similarity in the data significantly reduces vulnerability to various forms of artificial manipulation, thereby suggesting that more conventional training techniques, like cross-validation, can offer substantial protection against such alterations. Furthermore, our analysis of the effects of data augmentation and the use of ensemble methods reveal that these methods are highly effective in regularizing the models and providing natural protection against adverse inputs. Our comprehensive study of the study design, data processing, model selection, and the models themselves reveal that our findings hold across various scenarios.

The nonlocal conservation laws with flux functions defined through the convolution of a kernel and a solution, represent various types of traffic flow and have been extensively studied, however they have also been modelled in alternative ways. A novel framework based on a nonlocal Lagrangian has been proposed, allowing for a more detailed analysis of these systems and making it possible to draw a precise connection between them and traditional systems with local flux functions. Utilizing this framework it has been proven that nonlocal systems converge to a system with a measure-valued solution in the limiting case where the kernel's support approaches zero and also that, under specific conditions, this convergence happens at a quantifiable rate. Moreover, a new class of entropy admissible solutions has been defined and it has been shown that solutions of the nonlocal systems satisfy this criteria and also converge to a measure-valued solution in a nonlocal version of a PDE that measures how quickly the solution converges to this limit.

A dilation surface can be visualized as a surface with varying scaling rules that preserve orientation, obtained by quotienting a finite area surface with specified dilation rules. Its structure is defined by a dilation equation derived from an invariant 2-form and a 1-form, and a key result from a recent paper establishes that generic dilation surfaces feature a specific type of dynamics, known as Morse-Smale dynamics. This study explores the topological implications of this result, revealing that a dilation equation's specific properties - being non-resonant and non-Markovovian - correspond to a topological equivalent of a specific graph structure, consisting of horizons and saddle points, and that these properties also indicate the presence of specific topological features such as cyclic structures and parallel-saddle-horon cycles.

Recent studies have highlighted the limitations of traditional functional connectivity measures, such as Pearson correlation and partial correlation, in analyzing brain networks. These issues stem from their inability to capture complex signal dependencies. A new approach is proposed to model brain connectivity using total correlation (TC), a more comprehensive dependency measure. Based on TC values derived from fMRI data, a new network is constructed and compared to traditional networks. Results show that the new network provides a more accurate representation of brain connectivity. A method is developed to visualize brain regions and their connections in a three-dimensional brain model. TC values enable the identification of brain regions with different dependency patterns. Furthermore, a method utilizing TC values for detecting epilepsy foci is explored and yields comparable results to previous studies based on partial correlation.

The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores three key Hilbert space unitary 
isomorphisms that explain the dual nature of functions represented by polynomials, 
power series, and ordered tensor products. This study generalizes this concept by 
incorporating the extensive array of Clifford algebras to develop a more comprehensive 
mathematical framework, yielding new insights into polynomial power series 
isomorphisms within these Clifford contexts.

In this study, a concept of Gaussian process conditioning based on the trajectories of a Gaussian random field is introduced. This concept is built upon the usage of a gauge as a function. The article derives the mean and covariance functions of the resulting conditioned Gaussian process. Additionally, the article proves that the conditioned process has pathwise continuity, a result that relies on a variant of the Chen-Robbins-Striezer inequality. The continuity result is further extended to include the application of the Borel-Chebyshev inequality in establishing almost sure Hölder continuity. The effectiveness of the approach is illustrated with examples.

This research investigates the wireless connectivity of a network consisting of stationary ground sensors and mobile air sensors. We examine the ground sensors' coverage through spherical clouds of airborne sensors and establish existence and continuity principles for the resulting connectivity probabilities. Furthermore, we provide explicit expressions for numerical analysis and derive asymptotic behavior for large and dense networks. We also discuss the influence of the spherical cloud's radius on connectivity probability and our numerical findings illustrate the parameter-dependent characteristics.

The last 15-20 years have been a transformative era for neutrino physics,
characterized by significant breakthroughs in particle classification,
quantitative evaluation of three-neutrino mixing parameters, and the discovery
of a non-zero neutrino mass. This progress, however, has laid the groundwork for
an even more exciting phase of physics, particularly through groundbreaking
research initiatives like CPON, NO$\nu$A, T2K, and DUNE. The upcoming DUNE
experiment, the premier long-baseline neutrino facility, will capitalize on this
progress by pursuing a highly precise exploration of neutrino phenomena.
DUNE, a massive, multi-university international endeavor, will be situated at
Fermilab and utilize a 52 kton Liquid Argon detector along with an exceptionally
powerful 2.4 MW proton accelerator, enabling it to analyze data from several
distinct sources. The experiment's ambitious goals extend to identifying neutrino
oscillation characteristics, resolving mass hierarchy issues, determining
neutrino-related variables, and investigating exotic physics, such as those
related to matter-antimatter asymmetry and sources of neutrino masses.
This white paper serves as a comprehensive overview of the DUNE project,
focusing on the experiment's precise exploration of neutrino phenomena, as
well as its technological innovations, construction progress, and anticipated
research outcomes.

Research on top tagging has shown significant growth in the past few years,
with recent studies employing Machine Learning techniques to enhance their
accuracy. This work focuses on understanding and analyzing the effectiveness
of specific sub-jet observables when integrated into deep neural models.
In particular, we investigate the distinct contributions of different
sub-jets, utilizing the Shapley value framework to isolate and evaluate
the impact of individual sub-jets on overall performance. This analysis
reveals that each selected sub-jet primarily targets top particle identification,
while also highlighting competing criteria. Furthermore, we identify previously
unrecognized sub-jets' potential in discriminating between top particles and
backgrounds.

This document establishes the fundamental elements for describing Virtual Organizations, referred to as VOs, and introduces a logical framework to describe their basic characteristics. It also covers more complex features, such as vo:billing, and vo:confidentiality, by integrating the description of refinement. The document is supported by a set of examples, as well as proofs of key principles, including uniqueness and consistency of certain model properties. The document has been formulated using the OWL Ontology Web Language.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents often utilize extensive historical data. However, standard methods like Q-learning and actor-critic algorithms tend to underutilize available information. In contrast, GAIL, a discriminator-based approach, employs an experience replay buffer to store observations and process them sequentially. This study proposes integrating an experience replay mechanism into traditional methods, enabling the offset of the previously disregarded benefits. Specifically, we develop and evaluate Variance Reduction based Experience Replay (V-REX), a novel approach designed to reduce the impact of high data variability on the accuracy of function estimation, leading to more efficient learning with smaller sample sizes. Our results demonstrate that incorporating V-REX significantly improves the efficiency of function estimation and accelerates learning in both discrete and continuous control tasks.

Two new strategies have been proposed for integrating certain types of Gaussian actions associated with matrix groups in various dimensions. This paper compares the newly introduced superbosonization formula with the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, using the orthogonal group's unitary and orthogonal determinants as a test case. It's discovered that the superbosonization formula is more efficient, simpler to apply, and results in lower dimensional integrals. This discovery is further extended by showing that superbosonization offers a more streamlined approach to computing the partition function in supersymmetric Yang-Mills theories, specifically in a large-N limit.

This paper introduces MoDeRNN, a detailed motion representation called Motion Dynamics, and a corresponding learning model called Dyanamic Recurrent Neural Network. Unlike existing methods, MoDeRNN's dynamic motion details are naturally adaptable to various objects, and its associated neural network is capable of learning the intricate motion patterns of objects without being over-influenced by background motion noise, thanks to its novel Dynamic Memory Recurrent Neural Network architecture. Furthermore, the use of a dynamic memory recurrent neural network in MoDeRNN significantly enhances its computational efficiency, reducing the processing time to half of state-of-the-art methods, specifically Mirror Pixels, by eliminating the latter's reliance on computationally expensive matrix multiplication. Comprehensive experiments on diverse human motion prediction tasks, using human joint motion data, validate the efficacy of MoDeRNN and the MoDeRNN MoRA method against the existing state-of-the-art methods Mirror Pixels, ST-Mixer, and Mixture of Experts.

This research focuses on alleviating the burden on Rust developers by introducing a user-friendly and efficient abstraction called Josephine, allowing seamless integration with JavaScript frameworks such as Node.js. By utilizing abstraction, Josephine simplifies memory management for frequently employed data structures including arrays, vectors, and matrices. Our evaluation of Josephine indicates notable improvements in efficiency, with method execution speed acceleration of up to x17 for typical cases. Furthermore, Josephine enables faster array creation, reducing execution time by x1.7, and facilitates more efficient vector and matrix operations, as evidenced by x1.4 performance boost in methods like multiplication and subtraction.

Theoretical physics is exploring the concept of neutrinoless double-beta decay, specifically how it's linked to high-energy particle collisions in accelerator-based experiments. This study examines how the neutral current interaction and the masses of Higgs bosons influence this process when considering a single type of neutrino, taking into account multiple sources of neutrino mass. Calculations demonstrate that these influences can significantly alter the probability of this decay at colliders, with variations potentially reaching up to tenfold. This study also examines how these effects vary depending on neutrino mass and the parameters that define it, including the mass of the Higgs boson and the energy level of the colliding particles. This research has significant implications for future accelerator-based experiments aimed at understanding neutrino properties and the ultimate composition of neutrinos as Majorana fermions.

Recent research has introduced polar codes with low density generator matrices (LDGPs) and complex belief propagation (BP) decoding techniques. A novel polar code, incorporating the BP decoder, has been developed. It exploits the close connection between BP decoding and polar codes to achieve better error correction performance, surpassing LPD and other enhanced BP decoding methods. The proposed code's capacity approaches Shannon's capacity limit, allowing for a simpler and more efficient design process than conventional polar codes.

We investigate the connections between the point spread functions (PSFs) of individual images and their sum, particularly through their moments. Our research provides general formulas for the first few coadded image moments and their corresponding variances, given the moments of the individual images. These formulas are developed using a series expansion and can be applied to any set of coadded images, regardless of the method used to obtain them, such as imaging with lenses or sensors that resolve individual pixels. Our analysis is valid under the assumption that coadded exposures involve unaltered, independent, and identically distributed, and non-negative, and coadded images with Poisson distributed values. Our research shows that matching the first two coadded image moments is generally sufficient for accurate deconvolution in most practical applications. We utilize the derived formulas to create simple metrics for estimating the local effective exposure time from measurements of coadded images, thereby providing straightforward metrics for deconvolution that rely on easily accessible, global parameters. We support our research with examples from actual astronomical images and simulated data.

This paper outlines the development of a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the fracture toughness of crystalline materials at a micro-level, taking into account various fracture mechanisms, grain boundaries, and an extensive range of grain sizes, starting from the grain size threshold up to several thousand times its limit. Through the simulation of fracture in samples with controlled micro-structures through the use of the phase-field fracture method, significant insights into the fracture of quasi-brittle - and fully brittle - solids at a micro-level are provided. Our findings also underscore the importance of considering the coexistence of multiple fracture mechanisms when analyzing and predicting how real solids, with their complex internal structures, respond to stress. Furthermore, the theory reveals that the observed variability in experimental data on fracture toughness can be attributed to the inherent stochastic nature of fracture in disordered structures, and demonstrates how our theoretical framework can be used in conjunction with our direct measurement method to establish a thorough, internally consistent understanding of the various length-scales governing the fracture of these internal structure-containing solids at a local level, and to predict how these scales affect fracture toughness in this range of grain sizes.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane along with correlated Gaussian free fields. This concept was initially explored for one dimension, but a theoretical framework has now been developed to handle higher-dimensional cases. Specifically, a new approach was formulated for pairs of doubly connected components, with potential implications for understanding random conformal block structures in theoretical physics.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm, in an intermediate timescale.

The challenge in offering practical benefits from large-scale quantum computation lies in convincing non-technical stakeholders, particularly those familiar with classical methods, about computation results without incurring significant overhead. We've successfully addressed this issue by developing an efficient classical verification method, significantly shortening the overhead from previously 2^{\tilde{O}(n)} to 2^{\tilde{O}(log^*.N)}. This innovative method, initially presented in arXiv:1801.0005, enables classical users to efficiently validate quantum computation outcomes, thus enhancing the trustworthiness of quantum services.

A blockchain is a centralised ledger that records and verifies all transactions within a network. Due to its secure and transparent features, it is suitable for applications that demand high trust levels. To support these features, consensus protocols verify transactions within the network, although these protocols require significant computational resources, which may hinder performance in large-scale IoT networks with resource-constrained devices. In our work, we propose a new approach to improve IoT performance by offloading complex operations to a dedicated gateway device and a centralised point of contact, which provides external data to the gateway. This design, based on the shared architecture of the Ethereum platform, demonstrates improved scalability and efficiency while preserving the security properties of IOT networks. We validate our solution in a food supply chain application to track products from production to delivery and eliminate the risk of counterfeit goods. Our approach combines these lightweight designs with existing blockchain features to ensure security and data integrity.

Generative models have become a vital component of modern machine learning, particularly in tasks requiring data generation. In this work, we examine a generative model that utilizes the SIREN generative architecture in conjunction with an implicit representation of cell shapes. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first time that cell shapes have been successfully generated using implicit representations. We address two primary challenges: training the model on manually drawn shapes, and the influence of varying level sets on shape perception. We overcome the former challenge by incorporating human-annotated boundary noise, and an loss function that prioritizes boundary information. We resolve the latter issue by training the model on noisy boundaries, thereby mitigating the impact of level sets. We confirm the model's performance through a comprehensive analysis, showcasing its ability to generate diverse, realistic living cell shapes.

Blind, low-vision, and other print-disabled individuals face unique challenges accessing digital documents. Current document management systems are often inadequate, making it difficult for these individuals to effectively navigate files. We introduce a novel Document Navigability factor to supplement the traditional Yuskei factors and develop a factor-level model to improve document navigability. Our research yields a set of 27 items to measure document navigability, which is then validated through both blind and able-bodied participants. Notably, highly correlated item sets emerge as a Direction of Movement, and factor scores calculated from these items correlate positively with basic computer skills. Our prDAF questionnaire is made publicly available to facilitate accessible document navigation for print-disabled individuals.

We introduce XLPretraining, a new language modeling task that unifies the benefits of language modeling and permutation auditing, but avoids the issues from both. This leads to improved performance, with XLPretraining being 3-13 times more effective than BERT on various benchmarks and 1-2 times 15-19% better than XLPretraining's later version. To unify these benefits, we've adopted an autoregressive approach like XLPretraining, but given that both left and right contexts are available in permutation auditing, we've incorporated additional data from augmented sequences into XLPretraining, using a novel masked position-indicated objective and a two-stage training method. This enables XLPretraining to 1.5-2.5 times 10-20% the 18-20 % XLPretraining's latest version.

We've developed an innovative approach for analyzing the transit spectra of stars surrounding exoplanets, which effectively utilizes both the stellar and planetary spectral features at high resolution. This method is particularly useful for identifying water vapor, as we've compared it to a standard approach that uses lower-resolution spectra. We've applied our technique to simulated spectra from habitable zone planets orbiting sun-like stars, as well as to actual stellar spectra, demonstrating its potential for accurate atmospheric measurements.

We will explicitly construct conformal metrics with constant curvature on Riemann surfaces featuring singularities using ODE derived from a type of meromorphic 1-form. This approach will have an application in classifying a type of metric with constant curvature on the 2-sphere, specifically those with two conical singularities, which is analogous to a theorem initially applied to metrics with one conical singality.

Research into the swimming mechanics of the centipede Centruroides acanthScaptus has revealed a significant role of the antennae as rudders when the insect is small. Our study, involving high-speed video recordings of the spider as it crosses water surfaces, showed that the antennae are actively moved out of water in a non-symmetrical pattern to correct the insect's direction. This movement is most pronounced when the spider is small, but diminishes as it grows heavier. Mathematical modeling and analysis revealed that the antennae are crucial in reducing drag and water reaction forces when the spider is light, but this role diminishes as its weight increases. This finding underscores the importance of the insect's size in its swimming technique and the underlying physical principles at play.

The ultimate goal of this project is to develop adaptive simulations capable of modeling tsunami propagation following an asteroid impact, which generates a massive wave in a low-density environment and allows for complex phenomena such as wave dispersion, diffusion, and angular spreading. To achieve high resolution in these situations without incurring prohibitively high computational costs, adaptive mesh techniques are employed. These methods dynamically adjust the size of grid cells, typically using an initially coarse uniform grid and adapting it based on either an adaptive refinement process that places finer grid cells near the wave source or an adaptive mesh adaptation process that moves and adjusts grid points in response to the spreading wave. Two adaptive mesh techniques, namely Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) and Adaptive Mesh Adaptation (AMA), are examined and compared. Two distinct grid adaptation criteria are also investigated: one uses a spherical wave function to mark grid cells near the wave source, and the other employs a moving marker that tracks the simulated wave. Two high-order accurate numerical methods are used to solve the shallow water equations: an Lax-Wendrof type Lax-Friedrichs Runge-Kutta method and a Finite Volume Method. This study successfully demonstrates that these techniques effectively simulate large-scale tsunami waves following an asteroid impact, producing a scattered and dispersed wave that is consistent with observed wave phenomena.

Recent observations from ALMA have identified a set of massive galaxies at redshifts between 4 and 6 that emit little to no optical light, in contrast to typical high-redshift galaxies. This unusual discovery is further explored in this study through the use of data from the "JWST Deep ALMA Legacy" project, which revealed the JADES-GC-G10-3 galaxy as the most distant known of these 'infrared-dark' galaxies, located at a redshift of 6.51. Notably, JADES-GC-G10-3's massive stellar population, in the range of 10^8-10^9 solar masses, has been detected by the NIRCam instrument on the James Webb Space Telescope, in spite of its lack of optical light. This challenges the notion that dust is the primary factor in suppressing optical light in galaxies at the early universe. The findings from this study suggest that a combination of small-scale and diffuse dust, rather than large, dense dust clouds, is responsible for absorbing the optical light from massive galaxies, in line with three-dimensional models of dust distribution predicted by simulations of galaxy formation and evolution.

The investigation into holographic superconducting models based on five-dimensional gravity and its associated small black holes led to the exploration of analogous theories framed in seven-dimensional gravity, incorporating both Chern-Simons and Einstein-Horndeski terms. This 7D gravity model is derived from a corresponding string theory with a massive abelian gauge field on a calibrated three-sphere, which was embedded in a background with a complex geometry of S^2 x Σ^3. The resulting 4D CFT exhibits self-consistent thermal phase transitions, which are triggered by the interplay between the photon's mass and an external vector field.

In a long and narrow container with horizontal axis, two types of disks with varying sizes and weights are placed in an alternating sequence. This container is sealed by movable pistons which ensure the equilibrium state is maintained. By adjusting the pistons, we can study how self-organization of the disks is affected by different compression levels. Using computer simulations, we examine this equilibrium state and find that smaller and heavier disks tend to sink to the bottom of the container. As a result, we observe the formation of distinct layers where each disk type is arranged according to its weight. This configuration is stable as long as there are no pistons present. However, once a piston is introduced, we find that smaller disks tend to stack on top of larger disks, creating a new, balanced arrangement. This unique stacking pattern is visible under specific ratios of disk sizes and weights. In the general case, we find a local minimum in the system's free energy, which corresponds to a stable equilibrium state. This free energy can be described as the sum of the system's potential energy and configurational entropy. Our analysis reveals that multiple local minima exist in the system's free energy, which suggests a complex internal organization of the disks.

Investigating the impact of El Nino-Southern Oscation (ENSO) variations on global precipitation patterns, researchers analyzed two-implementing datasets, focusing on the frequency of extreme precipitation events during distinct flavors of ENOS. Their analysis, which covered the period from 1980 to 2014, revealed a significant shift in precipitation patterns in response to different flavors of ENSO. Notably, the intensity of low and high precipitation events varied significantly, particularly in tropical regions, with a notable 2.5 times increase in low precipitation frequency and a 1.5 times increase in high precipitation intensity during distinct flavors of ENSO. Furthermore, the study found that low precipitation frequency decreased in response to both high and low precipitation intensity, which challenges the proposed mechanism of the "reverse ENSO" mechanism.

A new method using polarized white-light scattering has been developed for monitoring the structural changes within solid materials as they respond to mechanical stress. This technique allows for real-time analysis of how the material expands and contracts at various levels, from a sample as a whole to a specific area with high precision. Utilizing the inelastic light-scattering effect, also known as Raman effect, this technique can directly compare how the atomic bonds in the material expand and contract in relation to the applied stress, without the need for calibration or complex calculations. This method was applied to diamond and diamond-analog materials, and was able to show how the material expands and contracts at different levels of stress. It was found that even materials that appear uniform at the surface exhibit noticeable changes in their internal structure under high levels of stress. This technique was also used to create detailed maps of how the material expands and contracts at the surface, and can be applied to other systems that undergo stress-induced changes, such as those used with high-resolution imaging techniques.

This research focuses on developing a population model that considers three factors: age, population density feedback, and environmental pollution. The model is expressed as a system of partial differential equations, and the existence of weak solutions is proven using the method of contraction. By applying the method of steps and an iterative technique, the primary outcomes of the study are obtained. Additionally, the long-term behavior of the model's solutions is analyzed using the theory of positive compact linear operators and a fixed point alternative. Furthermore, a novel approach based on a novel weakly continuous operator is introduced to establish the existence and uniqueness of non-trivial long-term periodic solutions, with an application provided as well.

The researchers achieve decidability for an infinitely large group of axiomatic extensions to the Full Lambek logic, specifically those with weakening and contraction properties, by developing a comprehensive hypersequent calculus and paired with an existing theorem on finitarity. Additionally, they calculate the complexity levels for the resolution methods and hypersequent calculus, finding the former to be NP and the latter to be PSPACE, respectively.

Hierarchical classifications like taxonomies are beneficial in numerous AI and human systems, employing nodes to depict concepts and edges for defining relationships, such as hypernymy, between concepts. However, the development of taxonomies is a labor-intensive process, and the static nature of their entries can hinder their applicability in tasks like search, where dynamically discovered topics and phrases are constantly emerging. To address these issues, researchers have proposed leveraging hyperbolic representation learning to model the inherent hierarchical characteristics of the concepts and their interconnections. In this study, we introduce HyperExpan, a text representation learning-based taxonomy expansion method, which generates new taxonomy entries by training machine learning models on the taxonomy and accompanying datasets. HyperExpan outperforms existing state-of-the-art taxonomy expansion methods by 10.8% in the F1-score, according to evaluations on four public datasets.

A molecular theory of the forces in electric fields is developed. The theory relies on the molecular composition and demonstrates the degrees of freedom in electric fields. The findings indicate that the various intermolecular forces are altered in electric fields. The molecular orbitals play a significant role in electric fields. A comparison of the dimers' behavior in electric fields and the isolated molecules' response to electric fields is also conducted. The dimers exhibit unique characteristics in electric fields. The dimers exhibit a greater sensitivity to electric fields than the isolated molecules. The results of this study are validated by the calculations using the ab-initio DFT method. The fourth Industrial Revolution has significantly improved manufacturing processes, particularly in areas like predictive maintenance and quality control, thanks to advanced data-driven methods. However, manufacturing involves inherent uncertainties that traditional analyses fail to account for accurately. A novel uncertainty-based scheduling model has been developed to tackle this issue in the manufacturing industry, utilizing data from a real case study to test the model's effectiveness in the metalworking sector. By incorporating both deterministic and non-cumulative probabilistic uncertainties, the model was able to achieve a high level of accuracy in its predictions, outperforming traditional scheduling methods and offering more realistic estimates of completion times. This improved modeling capability has the potential to pave the way for further advancements in the integration of smart manufacturing technologies.

This article introduces a novel concept of resilience for Cyber-Physical Systems, rooted in the theory of temporal logic. This framework enables a deeper comprehension of resilience characteristics and facilitates a detailed examination of the relative significance of different properties. Furthermore, this formulation is not system-specific and can be easily adapted to accommodate the unique requirements of various Cyber-Physical Systems. To illustrate the utility of this approach, several examples are provided, highlighting the advantages of a formal and customizable definition of resilience.

One of the most pressing enigmas in modern physics is the existence of dark matter. Although it's confirmed that dark matter gravitationally influences stars and galaxies, this unknown matter remains a significant puzzle. One way to study this phenomenon is to use accelerometers, sensitive instruments that can detect minute forces. Large networks of these devices, initially designed to monitor earthquakes, tsunamis, and other natural disasters, can now be repurposed to search for dark matter. This article outlines a comprehensive dark matter experiment utilizing existing seismic networks, focusing on this study's novel aspects, such as the development of a simulation tool to model dark matter-induced signals and the examination of noise patterns in these networks. So far, this research has successfully detected galactic tides and dynamical effects within the underground environment, as well as setting limits on sub-GeV mass dark matter interactions with nucleons up to 10^-14 cm. Accelerometer networks, with their ability to operate continuously over vast areas, offer significant advantages over traditional dark matter detectors. Future searches aiming to further constrain sub-GeV mass dark matter interactions and potentially discover new dark matter particles can be easily conducted using these networks.

This study derives a long-term Hamilton-type gradient estimate for a generalized nonlinear diffusion equation on complete, weighted Sturm-Liouville metric spaces. The investigation builds upon previous work by Li and Song, who established similar estimates for a nonlinear heat equation with an external force on complete Riemannian manifolds with a lower Ricci curvature. Their work led to the derivation of Harnack inequalities and further insights into heat equation solutions. The current research extends this work to a nonlinear diffusion equation with an external force, under the assumption of a modified Ricci curvature lower bound, and uses the maximum principle to derive the estimated gradient. Furthermore, the findings are applied to obtain local and global Harnack inequalities for a nonlinear diffusion equation, with the potential to generalize this work to include an external force.

Radio sources powered by jets may hold the key to understanding the distribution of radio luminosity across the universe. A study by Haverd et al. (2019) discovered a correlation between the sources' luminosity and the number of jets they contain, which they discovered by analyzing nearly 1,000 faint radio sources, which they stacked to examine the structures within them. Our research aims to understand how the sources' structures change as function of cluster radius, angular size, and flux density, which we achieve by breaking the sources into groups and examining their structures through stacking. Our findings reveal that jet-dominated sources with higher luminosity have stronger jet components and narrower beam patterns, whereas single-lobed sources have higher Alfv\'en speeds and narrower jet components as their luminosity increases. Furthermore, our study shows that jet-dominated sources with higher luminosity have higher velocities and less diffuse material, whereas single-lobed sources have higher fractional content of diffuse material. Our study also reveals that jet-dominated sources with higher luminosity have higher rectilinear shapes, whereas single-lobed sources have higher elliptical shapes.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical model, often used in bioinformatics and for analyzing audio signals, that have been applied to analyze how secret computations release information over time. In bioinformatics, HMMs are used to analyze DNA sequences, providing insights into the genetic traits of an individual. Our paper offers a new, more abstract model of HMMs, making it easier to understand how HMMs work in the context of information flow. This new model is based on category theory and makes HMMs a natural outcome of this mathematical framework. By using additional mathematical tools, like monads and Karoubi categories, we can create a more abstract model that is easier to work with. Our work also shows how HMMs can be used to create information flow systems, and how to analyze these systems using a mathematical tool called adjoint functors. This research has implications for understanding how secret computations release information over time, and for creating systems that protect private data.

We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport properties, where the flow field statistics are represented as a continuous time Markov process. This representation accurately captures turbulence's coherent structures responsible for transport, yet leads to complex partial differential equations. We then derive equivalent equations with traceless advection terms, where the stochastic elements are removed, and obtain closed equations for the mean transport quantity. Additionally, we create a closed system for the transport variance, representing the flow particle displacement. Our approach is applied to a specific case where the flow particle displacement follows a Gaussian process. We then generalize a previous result from [A. Chabanis and J. C. Hinch, Phys. Fluids 9 (1997) 109] to this model.

We maintain that many 'good' fits to elastic scattering data are unwarranted,
lacking a genuine understanding of the data. We claim that most successful
fits are achieved by increasing gluon density in protons, matching observed
cross sections at specific energies, but this approach fails to explain gluon
density in protons at lower energies through non-perturbative methods. The
approach using many gluons in protons also falls short of addressing binary
particle interactions correctly and produces energy-dependent cross sections
that contradict observations of gluon density in protons at higher energies.
An alternative theory, based on the concept of dipole-dipole scattering, is
introduced as a solution to these issues. This theory is grounded in the
behavior of non-diffractive reactions and predicts dipole-dipole scattering,
which contributes to elastic scattering. Notably, our cross section predictions
remain consistent across various energy levels, mirroring observed gluon density
in protons. Large proton structure is also incorporated into our elastic
cross section calculations. Large proton structure is supported by multiple
sources, including the Gerasimov-Dirac-Morehouse-Sommerfield sum rule, which
indicates significant proton radii up to 1 femtometer. Large proton structure
can be observed in the interference patterns of dipole-dipole scattering amplitudes.

This work examines the impact of Casimir's effect on the thermodynamic properties of black holes, focusing on the radiation within a closed space. A model has been developed to study the thermodynamic behavior of the system, with the aim of achieving equilibrium between the black hole and the surrounding space. A thermodynamic analysis is performed to investigate the implications of the model, with the resulting phase diagram depicting the phase transitions of the system within the pressure-temperature plane. The study reveals the influence of Casimir's effect on the phase transitions of the black hole within the space, with the critical points of the transitions being determined. A numerical analysis of the phase transitions reveals the conditions required for the system and the thermodynamic properties of the black hole within the space. A diagrammatic representation of the phase transitions is provided to illustrate the implications of the model, with the diagram showing the phase transitions of the black hole within the space, along with the critical points of the transitions.

Protecting users of location-based services, services, and apps from having their whereabouts tracked, involves understanding the risks associated with location logging. Our research introduces a new method for evaluating these risks and generating prior expectations about users' locations based on historical data, while also taking into account relevant conditions. A key feature of this approach is that it's more streamlined compared to the existing conditional maximum likelihood method, as it's only required when new data is introduced. Our study also demonstrates the incorporation of this approach within the framework of conditional maximum entropy. Furthermore, we develop the conditional posteroexpectation, which represents the updated expectations derived from the conditional posterior probability and is utilized in Bayesian inference. Finally, we demonstrate the application of these concepts in safeguarding the confidentiality of a specific individual's location by leveraging historical data.

A widely used 3D localization system, the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation, is becoming more prevalent due to its effectiveness. However, the traditional NDT localization method is still vulnerable to failures in more complex scenarios. A new method, NDT-Transformer, is introduced in this research to enhance the accuracy of 3D NDT localization by leveraging the benefits of self-attention mechanisms from the widely successful Transformer architecture. By incorporating multiple 3D localization cost maps into the Transformer encoder and using a delta-mechanism in the cross attention layers, the proposed method can produce more precise localization results. The NDT-Transformer method has shown superior performance on the NDT and KITTI benchmark datasets, accurately resolving scenarios where conventional NDT localization may fail. Furthermore, the proposed method has shown improved performance on real-world data, and the source code is available for public use on the GitHub repository https://github.com/136523210/NDT-Transformer.

The assessment of functional brain connectivity in research has predominantly relied on Pearson's correlation, a technique that often suffers from reduced statistical sensitivity in real-world applications. Real-world experiments frequently face limitations such as smaller sample sizes, intricate data collection processes across multiple sites, and other complexities that hinder significant discoveries. Our investigation into the effectiveness of various connectivity metrics in actual multisite datasets from the Human Connectome Project reveals that using a combination of metrics can enhance detection sensitivity in notable regions, including parts of the default mode network, despite producing comparable prediction accuracy to Pearson's correlation alone. Our research suggests that adopting a multi metric approach to functional connectivity is particularly advantageous for multisite datasets, and we offer practical recommendations for multiset analysis.

In a single-hop network operating on the 'listen' channel, we investigate the 'naming' problem, a more constrained version of the classic gossip problem. It's assumed that all nodes are connected and wake up simultaneously. Each node's unique name is shared through a beeping communication channel, a shared medium that only transmits short pulses or remains silent for both sending and receiving nodes. Both the transmitter and receiver can 'listen' or 'wake up' for incoming signals. If a node hears another's transmission, it confirms it's part of the same network and receives that node's name. If a node fails to detect anyone else's transmission, it remains silent and 'beeps' for its name only when woken up. It's also assumed that each node learns of every other node's name after the communication process concludes, and the goal is to find an efficient naming protocol in terms of total energy consumption and communication delay. It's shown that this problem is only solvable if at least $\log_{2}{n}$ nodes successfully 'gossip' their names to the entire network, and therefore only $ \Omega(n\log_{2}{n})$ node transmissions are necessary for this to occur. It's also demonstrated that $\Omega(n)$ node transmissions are sufficient for this purpose and a corresponding protocol is presented. It's shown that this protocol performs well for Poisson-wake up distributions, achieving $\Theta(n\log_{2}{n})$ total transmissions with high

Recent advancements in NLP have gained significant traction in areas like Indian Code-Mixed text, a form of language characterized by the blending of two or more languages in a single word, phrase, or sentence. Research has shown that switching between languages often occurs at a sentence level, but our study reveals multiple points of transition within a single sentence. We introduce a novel position encoding technique that leverages these transitions to represent changing language use accurately. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of combining this encoding with Transformer-based models, outperforming existing models on real-world datasets for tasks such as sentiment analysis, summarization, and cross-lingual summarization.

Using a combination of first-principles calculations and the Hartree-Fock-Allen-McMillan theory, we've analyzed the electronic structure and superconducting properties of H$_3$S under high pressure to understand its critical temperature's dependence on pressure and isotope mass. We've found that as pressure increases, the density of states at the Fermi level increases, as does its proximity to the van Hove singularity, correlating with rising critical temperatures. We've discovered that superconducting characteristics vary significantly with pressure, peaking around 200 Gb, after which they decline, a phenomenon also evident in the isotopic effect coefficient.

The effectiveness of motion planning in dynamic environments largely depends on whether a viable path exists within the environment's boundaries. Traditionally, motion planning algorithms have focused on avoiding static obstacles, but dynamic environments require consideration of the movement of obstacles as well. This study presents a novel approach that identifies traversable paths by taking into account the dynamics of obstacles, using a data-driven method to simulate obstacle movement based on real-world data such as the URBAN dataset, which includes dynamic simulations of urban street scenes. By analyzing the effects of various traversability constraints on both sampling-based and field-based motion planning algorithms, the paper demonstrates the feasibility of incorporating obstacle movement dynamics to improve motion planning in dynamic environments.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of images is initially created, linking 2D image features to 3D geometric information obtained through photorealistic rendering. By applying spatial mapping and temporal filtering, the method efficiently processes large-scale 3D maps. Learned descriptors are then utilized to quickly identify rough geometric models in real-time, enabling the refinement of model positions and normal vectors through surface matching and subsequent pose estimation via an iterative Kalman filter. Notably, with the rapid classification of model components, the method achieves faster visual relocalization by minimizing the search domain. The proposed approach is evaluated on two real-world datasets, 2D and 3D models, and demonstrates improved accuracy compared to a baseline method.

In the context of multiuser MIMO, the task of jointly selecting users and precoding can be reformulated as recovering a group-sparse signal from underdetermined equations. Building on this reformulation, the paper introduces an algorithm grounded in the group LASSO approach. Relative to the existing solutions, the proposed method achieves two key improvements: higher attainable sum-rate values and lower interference at inactive user devices. Moreover, the paper demonstrates that the group LASSO approach outperforms the sparse identification using prior information (SPIPRI) method in terms of sum-rate, while having comparable computational complexity.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular collection of divisors on the tropical curve that satisfy the Riemann-Shottlandy inequality, which can be done in finitely many ways. As a direct consequence, the rational function semifield is shown to be finitely generated over the tropical semifield, and this implies that the tropicalist ideal theory is applicable in this context.

This note focuses on estimating the speed of convergence from one step to a Q-process in discrete-time Markov chains. Initially, we assume the existence of an $\alpha$-H\"older invariant measure and establish a speed of convergence at the rate $\alpha$. Next, we relax this assumption, allowing for the approximation by an H\"older measure, and determine the convergence rate based on the modulus of continuity. We also apply our findings to Stark's problem.

We've demonstrated that combining the 1-cocycle of a long knot's space with Fox-Hatcher 1-cycles over rational coefficients creates a homomorphism from long knots to $ \mathbb{Q} $. Specifically, in knot spaces, the combination of this space's 1-cocycle with a particular Vassiliev invariant of order three produces the abelianized Fox-Hatcher cycle. Moreover, our work reveals an insurmountable obstacle in creating a universal Vassiliev invariant of order three that, when combined with a 1-cocycle, yields the 1-cocycle at a particular value equivalent to its own at any long knot's space.

Our study of the iron-based superconductor LiFeAs, which exhibits  T c  of 18K, has utilized single-crystal samples as low as 1.4T. By leveraging X-ray resonant elastic neutron scattering, we have shown that previous claims of nematic order in FeAs-based superconductors are unfounded. The absence of the observed lattice splitting in LiFeAs, stemming from its extremely low  T  of Li+, has enabled us to study the material's native symmetry. The anisotropic superconducting transition in LiFeAs has been found to align with a tetragonal-pseudogap behavior, in which the superconducting critical temperature,  T  c, is significantly lower than the pseudocritical temperature,  T  p, and subsequently,  T  c  is found to be approximately half of  T  p. This is evidenced by the emergence of the electromagnetic response, starting at  T  p, which is a few K above  T  c. The findings suggest that the presence of nematic fluctuations may play a significant role in enhancing  T  c  through a Nematic Superconductivity mechanism.

This research reviews a global analysis of Type-II two Higgs doublet models, focusing on how the Higgs coupling cluster parameter $\tan\beta$ influences allowed regions in the $m_A$-$m_H$ plane to evaluate the consistency of future collider findings within a single global fit. We incorporate the signal strength measurements from a future 3 TeV lepton collider and a 100 TeV hadronic collider into our analysis. Furthermore, the research includes the one-loop signal strengths of $h\to\gamma\gamma$ and $h\to\text{ZZ}$ decays from a future 1 TeV $\mu^+$ $\mu^-$ collider at 30 ab$^{-1}$ to refine our analysis within a type-II two Higgs doublet models framework. We show the implications of these measurements in a contour plot within the $m_H^0$-$m_A^0$ plane, similar to what is done in the MSSM, and surprisingly, our analysis indicates that almost all parameter space within both the low and high $\tan\beta$ regimes is consistent with the measured Higgs signal strengths when fitting the results from all three future colliders.

We demonstrate an autonomous learning method for manufacturing complex, self-assembling particle aggregates, which constitutes a form of artificial life. Our approach combines elements of deep reinforcement learning and genetic programming, enabling it to identify novel, intricate construction methods for targeted material structures. In exchange for minimal rewards, gradually increasing in difficulty, teaching agents create and refine reconfigurable assemblies out of individually mobile particles. A significant innovation in our method is the development of a novel protocol representation, which greatly enhances computational efficiency and allows novel, complex behaviors. Our approach is versatile and can be applied across a broad range of problems without the need for adjustments. It has successfully manufactured previously unknown, self-sustaining, and complex material architectures that surpass conventional thermodynamic stability principles.

Our research centers around a class of anomalies in chiral gauge theories, characterized by non-geometric, strong anomalies, which become increasingly prominent at high dimensions. This type of anomaly precludes quantum mechanics from being well-defined on any classical background, including manifolds. We devise an approach to strengthen an anomaly in gauge theory by introducing a gauge-dependent action, which generates a large action value due to large gauge transformations. This strategy allows us to decouple the gauge degrees of freedom and replace them with boundary degrees of freedom on a manifold with a boundary. Subsequently, we can formulate the theory as a non-dynamical boundary quantum field theory. Utilizing this approach, we can expand our understanding of anomaly inflow. Moreover, our work sheds new light on the phases achievable in chiral gauge theories, which can be gauged by representing them as boundary QFTs. We also demonstrate how anomalies can provide constraints on operator content in a quantum field theory.

We demonstrate that the stationary Navier-Stokes equations are ill-defined in specific, particular Besov spaces that are critical on both ends and in the semi-direct group of their scales. This novel outcome challenges previously established research and presents a contrasting paradox to recent discoveries in a broader class of Besov spaces at criticality. This study employs a refined framework involving interpolation techniques to examine long-standing questions regarding existence in Esakia's work and concerning particular Besov spaces at criticality discovered by Guo and Shu. This study also delves into open inquiries regarding uniqueness issues in various contexts and spaces.

We are investigating the dynamic properties of a magnon mode within an antiferromagnetic insulator. Focusing on a single non-reciprocal magnon branch, we pertain to samples with thickness on the order of the skin depth. A two-level system, when interacting with this magnon mode, introduces a strong nonlinear interaction. This coupling also facilitates a significant shift in the magnon mode's frequency. We are exposing the magnon mode to thermal excitation from its surroundings, observing a phenomenon where the magnon mode becomes thermally squeezed when exposed to thermal noise at temperatures exceeding the material's Néel temperature. Our research provides a foundation for developing magnon-based devices and exploring their use in quantum information processing.

This research introduces two modifications to Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem, built on the Gabidulin code structure, that address its known vulnerabilities, including a differential attack by Meier and Schreier and a structural threat by Bourdon-Moore and Loidreau. The revised system aims to provide an alternative option to current LPR codes, surpassing them in code length and rate while preserving equivalent security levels. Furthermore, we also provide a novel modification that addresses the aforementioned vulnerabilities, with a focus on short Gabidulin codes.

To pre-train cutting-edge language models like BERT, enormous, multi-terabyte corpora are necessary, leading to significant challenges in terms of processing requirements, storage, and energy consumption. To mitigate these issues, novel pre-training methods are being developed, focusing on utilizing shorter training sequences. One such approach involves expanding the model's vocabulary through the incorporation of word pieces. Despite this progress, previous models have struggled to accurately represent whole words. In response, our research proposes Dict-BERT, which incorporates a dictionary to divide the input into meaningful units. These units consist of words, subwords, and tags, with each tag indicating an error in spelling. By adding the subwords and tags to the model's vocabulary, our research shows that Dict-BERT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models, particularly in scenarios involving noisy inputs and shorter training sequences.

The minimum weight spanning tree in graphs and its higher-dimensional equivalents, known as minimal weight spanning acycles (MSA), are fundamental concepts in network analysis. These structures are derived from weight functions and can be used to represent data and compute persistence diagrams. MSA cycles and persistence diagrams from random complexes have been found to conform to Gumbel distribution laws, even in cases where the number of variables is correlated. This correlation arises when sampling from a fixed embedding or a random geometric graph. As a result, theoretical models can accurately predict the maximum weights in MSAs and provide useful bounds for real-world applications, such as predicting the maximum duration of persistent features in single-cell RNA-Seq data.

This new work reveals a未曾报道的威胁场景在垂直联邦学习的环境中，其中不同的
训练参与者可能通过联邦聚合过程窃取敏感数据从其他参与者，谁具有共同的
ID特征共享，谁接收更新后的模型头用于训练他们的本地模型梯度的剩余敏感信息.
我们证明，一个训练参与者能够成功窃取敏感目标ID，谁拥有相应的敏感目标ID梯度，
即使参与者已经泄露了他们的ID梯度中的ID部分，通过组合这些泄露的ID部分和聚合的模型更新.
该攻击利用了联邦学习中的共享ID特征和ML模型中的通用后门攻击技术，并实现了对目标ID的隐蔽训练，满足特定的泄露约束，包括ID目标部分的泄露和剩余敏感信息的目标ID梯度.
该攻击的核心组件是一个新颖的优化问题，用于优化每个参与者的本地模型更新，用于最小化总训练损失，同时满足特定的泄露约束，以及一个相应的分布式解决方案，用于每个参与者的本地优化.
实验结果表明，我们的攻击成功地实现了隐蔽数据在联邦学习的环境中，并导致了性能损失，同时揭示了攻击引起的性能损失与目标ID的敏感性和目标ID的数量的相关性.

A theoretical framework known as the light-cone sum rules is utilized to investigate the decay process where a B meson transforms into a proton and an uncharged dark antibaryon made up of dark antiquarks. This model includes a scalar pseudoscalar B meson composed of a light quark and its antiparticle, as well as a dark antibaryon adhering to the color-flavor locked configuration. By solving the twist-3 dark antibaryon distribution amplitudes via light-cone sum rules, the decay amplitude is determined along with its corresponding coupling constant. Calculations further reveal the into proton dark antibaryon decay rate, the B to proton dark antibaryon decay branching ratio, as well as the radiative B meson decay into a proton, dark antibaryon and two soft photons. These findings could potentially be observed at particle colliders such as the LHCb, ATLAS, CMS, and Belle II.

In a Smart City environment, vulnerable security systems can be exploited by malicious actors who may target both digital infrastructure and physical facilities. This paper models interactions between defenders and attackers in such an environment as a dynamic game where resources need to be managed strategically. The defense strategies are based on the capabilities of each entity and take into account various attack types. However, current approaches assume fixed resources, which may not be applicable in all scenarios. To address this limitation, we introduce a new game model that enables dynamic resource allocation for defenders and determines the optimal distribution of resources for both parties. The defense model is formulated as a multiple-choice knapsack problem and solved using heuristic algorithms, while a Monte-Carlo simulation evaluates the effectiveness of various attack-type defenses in different initial configurations.

Researchers discovered that the asymptotically AdS black holes can undergo Hawking--Page transitions at finite temperature when they are enclosed in a cavity. A key finding in this study is the appearance of "turning points" in the temperature, radius, and mass curves, which is due to a change in the slope of the radius and temperature curves, as well as black hole stability. Moreover, our study reveals that the thermodynamic properties of black holes in a cavity are influenced by a turning point and that these properties can be unique, including specific heat and entropy. Furthermore, the study also established that a cavity black hole can reach thermal equilibrium in two ways, one of which is through direct contact with a thermal bath, and the other, by finding "turning points" in the black hole radius and temperature curves. A notable feature is that the specific heat in a cavity can take positive or negative values, which can indicate local stability or thermodynamic instability, respectively. A particularly intriguing observation is that the specific heat sign change occurs twice, once when the black hole forms and once when it reaches a certain size.

Long document ranking in information retrieval is a critical challenge in NLP, especially in applications like in-depth knowledge search and medical diagnosis. Recent approaches for this challenge have shown that adopting a noisy-label classification technique, specifically the Balanced Sample and Group Loss (BSGL), can yield better results. However, NLP and information retrieval communities have been separate, with limited interaction between the two areas. This research bridges this gap by presenting the first application of the BSGL method in information retrieval, specifically in document ranking based on long forms. To achieve this, we introduce two new metrics to measure effectiveness in the information retrieval context, namely BSGL-oriented Mean Hit at K ("M Hik") and Balanced Sample and Group Loss Mean Accuracy ("BSGL OA"). To enhance efficiency, we also propose two new metrics to estimate the complexity of the ranking models by considering the size of input documents and by adapting the group loss by number of noise labels rather than by number of groups. Experimental results on two public datasets, TREC-QA and PubMed, show that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art information retrieval methods in terms of effectiveness and efficiency.

Recent research into few-shot learning has demonstrated significant potential for solving classification tasks, particularly when combined with a technique called pseudo-labeling. However, this approach is often hindered when applied to graph data, as seen in node classification. To address this challenge, we have developed a semi-supervised method tailored for graph data that enhances pseudo-labeling in this specific context. By utilizing graph neural networks, we prioritize labeled examples, effectively mitigating noise in pseudo-labeled distributions. In experiments with the benchmark datasets, our proposed approach has consistently outperformed state-of-the-art methods in node classification.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in the context of AWAKE experiment's advanced plasma wakefield acceleration offers a non-invasive means to analyze the transverse dynamics of trapped electrons. This research examines how spectroscopic analysis of betatron radiation can serve as a diagnostic tool by simulating the evolution of electron trajectories through numerical code. Furthermore, the study explores the impact of parameters such as observation angle and background noise from Hawking and Compton scattering on the resulting betatron radiation patterns, with a focus on the 2D intensity and power spectra generated in the AWAKE experiment's experimental setup for Run 2.

The growing need for privacy protection in cloud-based machine learning has led to the development of techniques for training privacy-protected models, with distributed learning being particularly challenging due to the requirement for multiple cloud interactions. The research addresses the privacy and accuracy concerns in learning privacy-protected decision trees by developing two novel algorithms. The first, DP-DT, involves each local model contributor training a privacy-protected decision tree while sending a truncated tree to a central central server for aggregation. The second, Federated DP-DT, utilizes a federated learning approach where contributors iteratively train and refine their local decision trees through multiple communication rounds. The algorithms' accuracy is mathematically proven in terms of the contributors' decision trees' depth and the privacy budget allocation. The experiments on various datasets show that both algorithms achieve accurate predictions.

We focus on a family of information distances known as the Bregman Hirsch-Renyi divergences and develop a broadened proximal gradient approach for their minimization. The standard algorithm struggles due to the differentiability limitations of their distance functions, so we propose a regularized version that can overcome these challenges under specific conditions on the underlying probability distributions. The proposed Bregman proximal gradient algorithm then becomes applicable for distributions that can be expressed as a mixture of a reference distribution and a kernel, and we also establish the rate of convergence under different parameter settings. The validity of this method in the context of the Bregman Hirsch divergences is further demonstrated through a comparison to a recently introduced alternative method for the same task. The performance of the algorithm is evaluated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world data.

This generalised form of Markov random fields allows for modelling data in chains and is particularly beneficial for pattern recognition. By incorporating prior distributions over graph structures using number of edges or vertices, we directly model potential graph models for observation data. We developed an extended Bayesian network for graph estimation which we adapted for graph models by modifying edge priors, then applied this to select the optimal graph model for a given dataset based on prior distributions over number of edges or vertices.

In a Hilbert space, we devise a continuous, damped dynamical system that converges to the Tikhonov regularized equilibrium for every positive regularization parameter, and we use this system to address the inverse problem of finding the element of the smallest norm within the pre-image of a given point. This method is innovative as it allows us to solve the pre-image problem without relying on iteratively decreasing the regularization parameter, a standard approach in physics. Instead, we use a two-stage process where the first stage finds a point within the pre-image and the second stage, starting from the first stage's solution, converges to the element of the smallest norm within that pre-image. This second stage is characterized by vanishing regularization parameters as time approaches infinity. We establish strong convergence towards the element of the smallest norm and provide rates of convergence. This method is effective for a broad class of problems and we demonstrate its efficiency with numerical examples.

This study investigates how slight changes in the behavior of a virtual wall-following robot lead to dramatic, unpredictable changes in its movement pattern. As we gradually increase the difference between the angles at which the robot turns left and right, its movement shifts from being confined within a limited area to being able to explore the entire map.
